rounds.analysis: Hypothesis: L21h6 is a successor head. Its OV maps an attended token to the next item; the oracle shows a 0.92 two-steps-ahead rate. In lookup prompts it barely attends to the queried value (0.01), while lookup heads do (L22h7, L21h8, L19h5, L16h14). So redirecting L21h6's QK from the final position to the queried value should make it emit the successor. The successor signal must also beat the copied value from the lookup heads. Round 1 tests three things: (A) QK rewiring alone with a modest gain; (B) the same plus silencing late lookup/copy heads; (C) the OV-transplant route, giving the L21h8 lookup head (attention 0.24) the successor OV of h6 while leaving h8's attention alone. Comparing A with C separates whether the bottleneck is attention routing or OV content.

candidates.rationale: Rewire L21h6 to attend from the final position to the queried value, using distance-independent low RoPE dims and an other_values contrast so it picks the queried line. Boost its output 2x so the successor competes with the copied value.

Same rewiring, plus removing the downstream/parallel lookup copy heads L22h7 and L21h8, so the literal value is not reinstated after the successor head writes. This tests whether copy competition limits the successor rate.

OV-transplant test: give the lookup head L21h8, which already attends to the queried value, the successor head's value/output weights. This leaves L21h6 intact for sequence continuation. If this works, the OV content is the key ingredient and attention routing is already adequate.

rounds.analysis: Round 1: rewiring L21h6 itself reached only 0.11 attention on the queried value. It gained just +10 points of successor rate and cost a lot: sequence continuation fell to 0.5 and WikiText loss rose 9%. Silencing the copy heads changed nothing, so competition from copied values is not the bottleneck. The bottleneck is the strength of the successor signal, meaning attention mass times gain. Transplanting h6's OV into L21h8 kept collateral damage low but gave only 0.095. New plan: build a dedicated successor head from a cheap head of layer 21, leaving h6 intact for text and sequences. Head 5 is a good choice: removing it costs -0.005 WikiText loss, and its group-mate h4 costs +0.001. I will use a sharper attention fit (ridge 0.01, rank 32) to raise attention above 0.11. The variants test dose-response through gain and through the number of parallel successor heads.

candidates.rationale: A dedicated successor head that keeps h6 intact. L21h5 is rewired final->queried_value with a stronger fit (ridge 0.01, rank 32, low band), given h6's successor OV, and its output is doubled. The reported attention will tell whether the sharper fit raises attention above 0.11.
Same as the first programme but with gain 4. This tests whether the successor rate scales with output magnitude once routing is fixed, and how much WikiText loss that costs.
Two parallel successor heads built from cheap heads h5 and h14, each at gain 2.5. Each head's attention is imperfect, so summing two heads should raise the successor signal while h6 stays untouched.

rounds.analysis: The attention fit B depends only on the layer input, not on the head, so the drop from 0.11 attention (ridge 0.1, rank 16) to 0.06 (ridge 0.01, rank 32) is a fitting effect. A sharper fit seems to overfit the word-value training prompts and transfer badly to ordinals. Untested hypothesis: stronger regularisation (ridge 1.0, rank 16) should raise attention. I also overlooked a side effect. h4 shares group 2 with h5, so it received both the rewired keys and h6's values, read out through h4's own output columns. That stray output may explain much of the WikiText damage, so every programme now silences h4, which normally costs about +0.001. P0 tests the ridge effect alone. P1 changes the contrast to other_positions, which should suppress attention to the sink and non-value positions. P2 skips fitting: it gives h5 the natural lookup QK of L21h8 (0.24 attention) plus h6's OV at gain 3.

candidates.rationale: Ridge test: same recipe as before but with ridge 1.0 and rank 16, which should generalise better from word values to ordinals. h4 is silenced to remove the garbage it outputs from the shared group.
Contrast test: other_positions should push attention away from the sink and non-value tokens, not only away from other values. Ridge is 1.0 and h4 is silenced.

Natural-routing test: h5 gets the QK of L21h8, an existing lookup head with 0.24 attention, plus h6's successor OV at gain 3. h8 and h6 stay intact and h4 is silenced. This shows whether borrowed routing gives a better dose-to-damage ratio than fitted routing.

rounds.analysis: Round 3 showed regularisation was the key. With ridge 1.0, attention on the queried value rose from 0.06 to 0.29, and to 0.35 with the other_positions contrast. The successor rate rose to about 0.41. WikiText cost dropped to 5.8% with the other_positions contrast, and sequence continuation was kept. Borrowing h8's QK gave no damage but a weak dose (0.18). The remaining limits look like (a) attention mass, (b) output gain and (c) the literal value still winning (lookup about 0.2). Silencing the copy heads did nothing in round 1, but the successor signal was weak then; it may matter now. Each programme changes one factor from the round 3 P1 baseline: other_positions contrast, ridge 1, rank 16, low band, h4 silenced, gain 2.5. P0 raises ridge to 3 to see whether attention keeps rising. P1 adds silencing of L22h7 and L21h8 to test copy competition. P2 raises gain to 3.5 to test dose versus WikiText cost; the budget allows up to 3.644.

candidates.rationale: Ridge trend test: ridge 1 gave a large improvement over 0.01. Does ridge 3 raise attention and transfer to ordinals further? Everything else matches the round 3 P1 baseline.

Copy-competition test: this is the baseline plus removal of the main late lookup copy heads L22h7 and L21h8. With a strong successor signal now present, suppressing the literal value may convert lookups into successors.
Dose test: the baseline routing with gain 3.5 instead of 2.5. This measures how successor rate trades against WikiText loss now that attention is about 0.35.

rounds.analysis: Round 4: ridge 3 raised attention to 0.54, yet the successor rate fell to 0.305 and WikiText damage grew. Over-smoothed keys probably catch spurious positions in ordinary text, so ridge 1 stays. Silencing the copy heads again did nothing, so copy competition is ruled out as the limit. Gain is the working lever. Gain 3.5 gave 0.50 successor at 3.577 WikiText loss, under the 3.644 limit. Loss grows superlinearly with gain (+0.18 from 1.5 to 2.5, +0.22 from 2.5 to 3.5), so the remaining headroom is small. This final round probes the edge of the dose curve and one untested damage lever, rank. P0 is the baseline at gain 3.7, a careful step toward the limit. P1 uses rank 8 at gain 3.5; a lower-rank QK should match fewer spurious patterns in WikiText, giving the same dose for less damage. P2 uses rank 8 at gain 3.9, which only becomes eligible if rank 8 really cuts damage.

candidates.rationale: Dose edge: this is the best recipe (other_positions contrast, ridge 1, rank 16, low band, h4 silenced) at gain 3.7. By extrapolation WikiText should land around 3.63, just under the limit, with a successor rate above 0.5.

Rank test: rank 8 at gain 3.5. A lower-rank attention map should keep the dominant final->queried_value direction while matching fewer spurious text patterns. Prediction: similar attention and successor rate, lower WikiText loss than 3.577.
Uses any damage saving from rank 8 to buy more dose: gain 3.9. It is eligible only if rank 8 substantially reduces WikiText damage. If so, it should give the highest successor rate.
